  a job at a software company here; the job is *why* she came. Gradually settling in.
- First-person narrator throughout (her own voice).

## Recurring cast
- **Nina** — Danish neighbour, met day 1 (week 1), Maya's first friend; lives in the same building. Kind, helpful.
- **Peter** — a colleague at Maya's software company; an easy, friendly workmate (met on her **first
  day, week 2**; recurs at the week-6 canteen lunch). Use him when a work colleague is needed rather
  than an anonymous *en kollega*.
- **Family** — back home in Mexico, contact by video call: parents (*mor/far*), sister **Sofía**,
  brother **Diego**, and the family dog **Lola** (siblings + dog established in wk3's family call).

## Cross-cutting rules (every week)
- **Privacy** — the CPR number is sensitive (like an SSN). Never read it out / repeat it digit-by-digit;
  treat it as private, kept safe. Phone numbers MAY be shared/read aloud.
- **Fictional data** — any phone number etc. must be an obvious placeholder, never a plausibly-real
  number. Maya's phone: **12 34 56 78** (*tolv, fireogtredive, seksoghalvtreds, otteoghalvfjerds*);
  Nina's: 87 65 43 21 (*syvogfirs, femogtres, treogfyrre, enogtyve*).

  for unrelated things in one scene (reads as if they're linked). A number **said aloud is written as
  Danish words, not digits** — this is an audio course (e.g. *tolv, fireogtredive…*, never *12 34*;
  times already use words like *klokken otte*).
- **Translation-robust** — avoid constructions that gloss/translate awkwardly (written-out abbreviated
  addresses, lexical ambiguities).
- **Dialogue** — speakers address each other correctly (a clerk speaks *to* Maya, not in Maya's voice).
- **Scene-to-scene flow** — where natural, a scene may foreshadow the next or pay off the previous; don't force a bridge on every scene.

scenes.scene: Maya opens the fridge and the cupboards in her new flat. The kitchen is completely empty. She grabs her reusable bags and heads out to the supermarket to buy groceries.
Inside the supermarket, Maya starts in the produce section. She examines the apples and the tomatoes, carefully selecting the ripest ones because she really likes fresh fruit and vegetables.
Maya walks over to the cold dairy section. She searches for the milk and the butter, comparing the different cartons until she finds the organic milk, which she likes best.
Smelling the bakery shelves, Maya decides to buy some traditional Danish bread. She picks up the heavy, dark rye bread, eager to try it, even though she also likes light, crusty rolls.
Maya steps up to the staffed deli counter. When it is her turn, she politely tells the shop assistant that she would like to have a piece of the aged cheese on display.
Missing the flavors of Mexico, Maya wanders down the international aisle. She hunts the shelves and finally spots the hot sauce, thrilled to find it because she really likes spicy food.
Maya leaves the store and walks back to her building. She carries the heavy grocery bags through the cold streets, excited to finally fill up her own kitchen.
Back in her flat, Maya unpacks the bags. She places the butter, the cheese, and the milk into the fridge, and she neatly arranges the fruit in a bowl on the kitchen counter.
Maya cooks her very first warm meal in the new apartment. She chops the vegetables, adds the cheese and the hot sauce, and sits at her table to eat, deciding she really likes the meal.

- 31, from Mexico. A **software engineer** — she moved to Copenhagen in **January** because she landed
  a job at a software company here; the job is *why* she came. Gradually settling in.
- First-person narrator throughout (her own voice).

- **Nina** — Danish neighbour, met day 1 (week 1), Maya's first friend; lives in the same building. Kind, helpful.

- **Family** — back home in Mexico, contact by video call: parents (*mor/far*), sister **Sofía**,
  brother **Diego**, and the family dog **Lola** (siblings + dog established in wk3's family call).

## Status ledger — what is TRUE by end of each week
### End of Week 1 (arrival)

- She does **NOT yet have**: a Danish phone number, a CPR number, an *official/registered* address.

Forcing the week's definite grammar target here will result in unnatural Danish that means 'I like these specific tomatoes on this shelf'.

response.issue: Accidental shoplifting
response.why: The narrative jumps straight from ordering at the bakery counter to carrying her groceries down the street. Even though the brief says 'no prices or amounts', skipping the checkout entirely makes it feel like she just walked out without paying.

response.issue: Basket vs. heavy bags mismatch
response.why: In scene 2 she grabs a single 'basket', but by scene 6 she is carrying 'heavy grocery bags' (plural). Given her relatively short shopping list, this feels like an exaggerated amount of luggage for what she actually bought.

scenes.scene: Maya stands in her flat, noticing that the fridge and the cupboard are completely empty. She grabs a large canvas bag and heads out, eager to buy food for the week.
Maya enters a large supermarket and picks up a basket. She walks straight to the produce section, as she really likes fresh vegetables and wants a healthy base for her dinners.
Among the familiar produce, Maya spots a strange, pale root vegetable. She realizes it is a parsnip, something she has never eaten before, but she drops it into the basket out of pure curiosity.
Moving to the bread aisle, Maya searches for a local staple. She likes dark, hearty bread, so she selects a heavy loaf of traditional Danish rye bread to try.
Maya stops at the staffed bakery counter for a sweet treat. She catches the eye of the baker behind the glass and politely asks that she would like to have a cinnamon pastry.

Realizing she still needs something for her morning coffee, Maya wanders around looking for the milk. Unable to find it, she stops an employee stocking shelves, who helpfully points her toward the cold dairy section at the back.
In the international aisle, Maya hunts for a comforting taste of Mexico. She smiles when she spots a familiar can of black beans, a food she truly likes, and happily adds it to her basket.
Maya brings her basket to the checkout line. She places her items on the moving belt, waves her card over the machine to pay, and quickly packs everything into her canvas bag.

Back in her flat, Maya unpacks the groceries on the kitchen counter. She organizes her space, placing the milk and the parsnip in the fridge, and setting the bread and the beans neatly in the cupboard.
With a stocked kitchen, Maya chops her vegetables and opens the beans. She cooks a warm, simple dinner on the stove, thrilled to finally eat a real meal in her own home.

issues.problem: In Danish, you do not generally 'lægge' (lay down) chopped vegetables and canned beans into a pot. It is much more idiomatic to use 'kommer' or 'putter' when adding ingredients to a pot (e.g., 'Jeg kommer maden i en gryde').

## Maya (protagonist)

- **Privacy** — the CPR number is sensitive (like an SSN). Never read it out / repeat it digit-by-digit;
  treat it as private, kept safe. Phone numbers MAY be shared/read aloud.

  Nina's: 87 65 43 21 (*syvogfirs, femogtres, treogfyrre, enogtyve*).
- **Numbers woven into action** (ages, tickets, house numbers), not drilled. Don't use the SAME number
  for unrelated things in one scene (reads as if they're linked). A number **said aloud is written as
  Danish words, not digits** — this is an audio course (e.g. *tolv, fireogtredive…*, never *12 34*;
  times already use words like *klokken otte*).
- **Translation-robust** — avoid constructions that gloss/translate awkwardly (written-out abbreviated
  addresses, lexical ambiguities).
- **Dialogue** — speakers address each other correctly (a clerk speaks *to* Maya, not in Maya's voice).
- **Scene-to-scene flow** — where natural, a scene may foreshadow the next or pay off the previous; don't force a bridge on every scene.
- **Translatable setting** — the real test is whether a place/thing **translates n-way**, not generic-vs-specific.
